readings.title: A Seat by the Window
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When Leena moved to a coastal town, she knew nobody outside the hotel where she worked. Her evening bus passed a bookshop with a handwritten sign: Bring a book, take a seat. She imagined a room full of confident readers discussing difficult novels. For three weeks, she remained on the bus. Then rain delayed her journey, and she stepped inside to get dry.

There was no discussion leader and no reading list. Six people sat around a table, reading whatever they had brought. A shop assistant explained that the first half hour was silent. Afterwards, anyone could mention a sentence or describe a book, but speaking was optional. Leena found a chair by the window and opened the inexpensive detective story in her bag.

At the next meeting, an elderly man named Tomas brought a notebook instead of a printed book. He had been recording memories of the town's old fishing harbour. Leena asked why one street had two different names in his account. Tomas explained that the name had changed after a storm destroyed the original bridge. Their conversation attracted a teenager who was drawing a map for a school project. Soon the three were comparing the notebook with a modern street map.

Leena still came mainly to read. She disliked the idea that every quiet activity needed a social purpose. Yet the predictable silence made conversation easier when she wanted it. Nobody demanded an interesting opinion, and nobody treated her detective stories as less valuable than other books.

Months later, a newcomer paused nervously in the doorway. Leena moved her coat from the spare chair. She did not ask what the visitor was reading. Instead, she pointed to the window seat and said, "You can start here." The small invitation reminded her how belonging had begun: with room to participate at her own pace.

readings.title: The Pause Between Practice Sessions
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A learner can repeat a new word so often that it begins to feel familiar. That feeling is pleasant, but familiarity is not the same as being able to produce the word tomorrow. When the word remains on the page, its visible shape provides help. Close the book, wait for a while, and the task changes: the learner must find the word in memory.

This distinction helps explain why short practice sessions spread over several days can be useful. A pause allows some details to become harder to recall. Trying to retrieve them then requires effort. If the learner succeeds, the act of retrieval gives another opportunity to strengthen the connection. If the attempt fails, checking the answer provides feedback about what still needs attention. A mistake during practice is therefore information, rather than proof that learning is impossible.

Spacing does not mean leaving every subject untouched for a week. The suitable interval depends partly on how well the material is known and when it will be needed. A complete beginner may need to return to a word later the same day. Someone who can already use it in conversation may benefit from a longer gap. Extremely long gaps can make practice frustrating because almost everything has been forgotten.

A practical routine combines brief review with a small challenge. Before opening yesterday's notes, write down three ideas you remember. Then compare your version with the notes and correct important omissions. Next, use one idea in a fresh sentence or example. This process asks more of memory than simply looking at highlighted lines again.

Rest, understanding, and clear explanations still matter. Spaced practice cannot repair material that has never made sense. Its value lies in arranging opportunities to remember, notice a gap, and try again. Progress may feel less smooth than repeated reading, yet that temporary difficulty can be part of useful learning.

readings.title: Must Every Meeting Be a Video Call?
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
For people who work in different places, a video call can turn distant colleagues into recognisable faces. Expressions and pauses may reveal uncertainty that a short message conceals. It is tempting, therefore, to assume that more video meetings always produce a closer team. Yet connection depends on the quality of attention, not simply the number of faces visible on a screen.

Consider a routine update containing three dates and a completed task. If everyone must stop work at the same moment to hear it, the meeting imposes a cost beyond its ten minutes. Someone loses a period of concentrated work; someone else joins at an inconvenient hour. A clear written update may convey the same information and leave a record that can be consulted later.

Written messages have limitations too. A difficult disagreement can grow sharper when readers imagine an angry tone that the writer never intended. A newcomer may hesitate to interrupt a busy message channel with basic questions. In such cases, a brief conversation can provide reassurance and allow an immediate explanation. The choice should follow the purpose, rather than a general rule favouring one tool.

Teams can make that choice easier by stating what a proposed meeting must achieve. "Discuss the project" is vague. "Choose between two delivery dates" gives participants something to prepare. When a meeting ends, a short written decision helps people who could not attend. It also prevents the group from having the same discussion a week later.

Social contact deserves its own space, but it need not disguise itself as compulsory business. An occasional optional conversation may be more welcoming than a daily call in which everyone must appear cheerful. A team becomes connected when its members can obtain help, understand decisions, and trust that their time matters. Cameras can support those conditions; they cannot create them by being switched on.

readings.title: Learning to Listen to the Machine
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
On his first morning at a furniture workshop, Daniel received a booklet describing each machine and its safety controls. He read it carefully, passed the required instruction session, and could name every switch. Nevertheless, when he began preparing boards under supervision, he felt uncertain. The booklet told him which measurements to check, but experienced workers seemed to notice problems before taking out a ruler.

His supervisor, Mei, did not ask him to work faster. She placed two finished boards side by side and asked what he observed. Daniel mentioned colour and length. Mei invited him to run a hand gently over the surfaces and look along their edges. One board felt slightly rough near the end. She explained how that small difference could affect the next stage of assembly.

For the following week, Daniel kept a question notebook. At first, his entries were general: "How do you know it is ready?" As he watched more closely, the questions became specific: "Why did you check this edge before measuring the width?" Mei could answer the second kind more easily because it referred to an action they had both seen. Daniel began adding simple sketches beside her explanations.

The notebook did not replace formal safety guidance, and Mei stopped him whenever a task required more instruction. Its purpose was to capture observations that were difficult to express in a general manual. Other workers later contributed examples, including occasions when a familiar method had failed because the material was different.

After several months, Daniel helped welcome another beginner. He showed her the booklet first, then asked her to compare two boards. He also explained that an experienced worker's quick decision often rested on years of noticing small differences. Learning such judgement took time. Asking a precise question was not an admission of incompetence; it was one way of making invisible experience available to someone else.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese.

Learning with another person does not mean moving at exactly the same speed. One learner may understand a new rule quickly, while the other remembers useful examples more easily. A successful partnership allows both people to contribute. Before each meeting, partners can agree on a small task and prepare separately. During the meeting, they explain their answers and ask about differences. If one person is uncertain, a patient question is often more helpful than an immediate correction. Over time, this habit can build confidence as well as knowledge. The aim is not to prove who knows more, but to help both learners take the next step.
translation.explanation: 仅供考生自评。注意while表示对照，as well as连接“信心”和“知识”，not ... but ...表达“不是……而是……”。参照意义完整、语言准确和表达自然三项标准评分。
translation.referenceAnswer: 与他人一起学习，并不意味着必须以完全相同的速度前进。一位学习者可能很快理解一条新规则，而另一位则更容易记住有用的例子。成功的学习伙伴关系能让双方都有所贡献。每次见面前，伙伴们可以商定一项小任务，并分别作好准备。见面时，他们解释自己的答案，并就不同之处提出问题。如果其中一人拿不准，耐心地提问往往比立即纠正更有帮助。久而久之，这种习惯不仅能增长知识，还能建立信心。目的不是证明谁懂得更多，而是帮助两位学习者都迈出下一步。

criteria.name: 意义完整
criteria.description: 准确传达全部主要信息与逻辑关系，不遗漏重要内容。

criteria.name: 语言准确
criteria.description: 词义、时态和指代处理准确，无严重误译。

criteria.name: 表达自然
criteria.description: 中文通顺，段落衔接清楚。

writing.stem:
Write at least 100 words in English on the following topic: A Learning Activity That Brings People Together.

Your community centre is collecting suggestions for a weekly activity open to adults with different ages, jobs, and levels of experience. Write a short proposal for the centre. Describe one activity that participants could learn together, explain how a typical meeting would work, and suggest one way to help a shy newcomer feel comfortable. Give a reason why your activity could help people develop both a useful skill and a sense of connection. You may use an imagined example. Do not write your real name or contact details.
writing.explanation: 仅供考生自评。范文提出手机摄影散步，说明活动流程、接纳内向新人的措施及技能学习和邻里联系两方面的收益。按任务完成、组织连贯、语言运用三项标准评分，不要求与范文使用相同活动。
writing.sampleAnswer:
I suggest starting a weekly photography walk at our community centre. Participants would only need a phone or a simple camera, so expensive equipment would not be necessary.

Each meeting could begin with a short explanation of one skill, such as choosing a clear background. We would then walk through a nearby park in small groups and try that skill. Afterwards, everyone could choose one photograph to discuss. The aim would be to share ideas rather than select a winner.

A shy newcomer could join an experienced volunteer and listen before deciding to speak. This would reduce the pressure to impress others. By observing familiar places together, participants could improve their photographs and discover shared interests. A simple activity might gradually turn neighbours who rarely speak into people who recognise and support one another.

criteria.name: 任务完成
criteria.description: 覆盖全部写作要点，内容具体且相关。

criteria.name: 组织连贯
criteria.description: 段落清楚，衔接自然，格式适合任务。

criteria.name: 语言运用
criteria.description: 词汇和语法基本准确，有适当句式变化。
